blocks.text: The conditional probability lesson showed that P(A given B) and P(B given A) are generally different numbers, and that swapping them by accident is one of the most common and most damaging mistakes in probability reasoning. Bayes theorem is the exact formula that relates the two directions to each other, and it is arguably the single most important formula in this entire probability module, powering everything from medical diagnosis to spam filters to how a machine learning model updates its beliefs as new data arrives.

blocks.alt: Bayes theorem combines a prior belief with new evidence to produce an updated posterior belief
blocks.caption: A prior, combined with a likelihood, produces a posterior

blocks.text: 1. From Conditional Probability to Bayes Theorem

The conditional probability lesson established the general multiplication rule in two equivalent forms, P(A and B) equals P(A given B) times P(B), and also equals P(B given A) times P(A), since joint probability does not care which event is written first. Because both expressions equal the same quantity P(A and B), they must equal each other.

Setting P(A given B) times P(B) equal to P(B given A) times P(A) and dividing both sides by P(B) gives Bayes theorem directly, a formula for P(A given B) written entirely in terms of the reverse conditional probability P(B given A) and the two individual, unconditional probabilities P(A) and P(B).

It is worth pausing on how small this derivation actually is, Bayes theorem adds no new probability rule of its own, it is simply the observation that a single joint probability can be written two different ways, once conditioned on A and once conditioned on B, and setting those two expressions equal to each other.
2. The Bayes Theorem Formula

Bayes theorem states P(A|B) equals P(B|A) times P(A), divided by P(B). Every symbol in this formula has a specific role, and getting comfortable naming each piece is the single most useful habit for applying the formula correctly rather than plugging numbers into the wrong slot.

code.content:
# Bayes theorem
# P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B)

def bayes(p_b_given_a, p_a, p_b):
    return (p_b_given_a * p_a) / p_b

posterior = bayes(p_b_given_a=0.99, p_a=0.01, p_b=0.02)
print(round(posterior, 4))

blocks.text: It helps to read the formula out loud in words before ever touching numbers, the posterior equals the likelihood times the prior, all divided by the evidence, a sentence worth memorizing since the rest of this lesson simply fills in what each of those four words means and where each number comes from.
3. Prior, Likelihood, Posterior, and Evidence

The four pieces of Bayes theorem each have a standard name that shows up constantly in statistics and machine learning writing, and mixing them up is an easy way to get lost in an otherwise correct formula.

items: The prior, P(A), is the probability assigned to A before seeing the new evidence B at all, the starting belief.
The likelihood, P(B given A), is the probability of observing the evidence B assuming A is true, describing how well A explains the evidence.
The posterior, P(A given B), is the updated probability of A after folding in the evidence B, the answer Bayes theorem produces.
The evidence, P(B), sometimes called the marginal likelihood, is the overall probability of observing B at all, regardless of whether A is true or false, acting as a normalizing constant.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: For the disease test scenario worked through in section 7 below, the prior is how common the disease is in the population, the likelihood is how often the test comes back positive on someone who truly has the disease, the evidence is how often the test comes back positive overall, and the posterior is what is actually wanted, the probability of having the disease given a positive result.

blocks.text: A useful way to keep the four terms straight is to notice that the prior and posterior both describe A, before and after the evidence respectively, while the likelihood and evidence both describe B, from the point of view of A being true and from the point of view of everything respectively.
4. Where the Evidence Term Comes From

P(B), the evidence in the denominator, is rarely given directly, it usually has to be built up from the law of total probability, splitting B across every possible value of A. For a simple yes or no event A, this means P(B) equals P(B given A) times P(A), plus P(B given not A) times P(not A), using the complement rule from the probability rules lesson to get P(not A).

code.content:
p_a = 0.01                 # prior, P(disease)
p_not_a = 1 - p_a          # complement rule
p_b_given_a = 0.99         # likelihood, P(positive test given disease)
p_b_given_not_a = 0.05     # P(positive test given no disease), the false positive rate

p_b = p_b_given_a * p_a + p_b_given_not_a * p_not_a
print(round(p_b, 4))   # P(positive test), the evidence term

blocks.text: This expansion of P(B) is itself just the addition rule from the probability rules lesson applied to two mutually exclusive cases, A true and A false, since those two cases cannot overlap and together cover every possibility, their contributions to P(B) simply add together with no double counting.
5. Bayes Theorem With a Table

A joint probability table makes every piece of Bayes theorem visible at once, since the prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior are all just different sums and ratios read off the same table, the same way conditional probability was read off a table in the previous lesson.

The prior P(disease) is the Disease column total, 0.0099 plus 0.0001, which is 0.01. The evidence P(positive test) is the Positive Test row total, 0.0099 plus 0.0495, which is 0.0594. The posterior P(disease given positive test) is the Disease and Positive Test cell, 0.0099, divided by that row total, giving roughly 0.167.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.0099, 0.0495],
                   [0.0001, 0.9405]])
prior = joint[0, :].sum()          # 0.01
evidence = joint[:, 0].sum()       # 0.0594
posterior = joint[0, 0] / evidence
print(round(prior, 4), round(evidence, 4), round(posterior, 4))

blocks.text: 6. Bayes Theorem in Code

The same table driven computation translates directly into a few lines of numpy, and this pattern, build a small joint table and read off a cell divided by a row or column total, is exactly the same technique the conditional probability lesson used, Bayes theorem has not introduced any new machinery, only a new way of assembling the pieces.

code.content:
import numpy as np
joint = np.array([[0.0099, 0.0495],
                   [0.0001, 0.9405]])   # rows: disease/no disease, cols: positive/negative
p_positive = joint[:, 0].sum()
p_disease_given_positive = joint[0, 0] / p_positive
print(round(p_disease_given_positive, 3))   # 0.167

blocks.text: This same handful of lines is the entire computational core of Bayes theorem, everything else in this lesson, the medical test, the spam filter, the naive Bayes classifier, is the identical calculation applied to a different labeled scenario, never a different formula.
7. The Medical Test Example: A Full Bayes Theorem Walkthrough

This is the single most famous illustration of Bayes theorem, and for good reason, it shows how badly intuition can fail without the formula. Suppose a disease affects 1 percent of the population, so the prior P(disease) is 0.01. A test for the disease is quite accurate, it correctly flags 99 percent of people who truly have the disease, so the likelihood P(positive given disease) is 0.99. But the test also has a false positive rate of 5 percent, meaning P(positive given no disease) is 0.05.
A patient tests positive. Most people guess the patient almost certainly has the disease, since the test seems accurate. Bayes theorem says otherwise.

code.content:
p_disease = 0.01
p_no_disease = 1 - p_disease
p_positive_given_disease = 0.99
p_positive_given_no_disease = 0.05

p_positive = (p_positive_given_disease * p_disease) + (p_positive_given_no_disease * p_no_disease)
p_disease_given_positive = (p_positive_given_disease * p_disease) / p_positive
print(round(p_disease_given_positive, 4))   # about 0.1667

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Even with a test that is 99 percent accurate on sick patients, a positive result only raises the probability of disease to about 16.7 percent, not anywhere near certainty. The reason is that the disease is rare, so out of every 10000 people, about 100 truly have it and about 99 of those test positive, but out of the remaining 9900 healthy people, 5 percent, or about 495, also test positive purely by false alarm. Positive tests from healthy people, 495, heavily outnumber positive tests from sick people, 99, so most positives are false alarms.

blocks.text: It is worth restating plainly why this feels so counterintuitive, most people anchor on the 99 percent accuracy figure and stop there, quietly ignoring how rare the disease is to begin with, but Bayes theorem forces the prior into the calculation whether or not intuition remembers to.
8. Why Rare Diseases Stay Unlikely Even After a Positive Test

The pattern in section 7 generalizes, whenever the prior probability of A is very small, the posterior P(A given B) stays modest even after strong evidence, because the denominator P(B) gets padded out by the far larger population of cases where A is false but the evidence still shows up occasionally by chance.

blocks.alt: Out of 10000 people, far more healthy people test positive by false alarm than sick people test positive correctly
blocks.caption: The 495 false positives outnumber the 99 true positives, dragging the posterior down to about 16.7 percent

blocks.text: This is exactly why doctors often order a second, independent confirmatory test rather than acting on a single positive result alone, since the section below on Bayesian updating shows how a second positive test can push the posterior up dramatically once it is combined with the first.
9. Bayesian Updating: Beliefs as Probabilities That Change With Evidence

Bayes theorem is often described as a rule for updating beliefs, the prior is a belief held before seeing new data, the posterior is the same belief revised in light of that data, and the likelihood is what carries the new data into the update. Crucially, a posterior computed after one piece of evidence can be reused as the prior for the next piece of evidence, letting belief update repeatedly as more data arrives.

code.content:
prior = 0.01
for observed_positive_test in [True, True]:
    likelihood = 0.99 if observed_positive_test else 0.01
    p_b = likelihood * prior + 0.05 * (1 - prior)
    prior = (likelihood * prior) / p_b   # posterior becomes the next prior
print(round(prior, 4))   # probability of disease after two independent positive tests

blocks.text: After a second independent positive test, the posterior climbs much higher than after just one, since each additional piece of consistent evidence multiplies further into the same running update, exactly the mechanism behind Bayesian inference in statistics and behind online learning systems that revise a belief as each new observation streams in.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Starting from a 1 percent prior, a single positive test raises belief in disease to about 16.7 percent, as computed in section 7. Feeding that 16.7 percent back in as the new prior for a second, independent positive test pushes the updated posterior above 80 percent, showing how quickly repeated consistent evidence can overwhelm even a very small starting prior.

blocks.text: 10. Bayes Theorem in Spam Filtering

Spam filtering is one of the oldest and clearest applications of Bayes theorem. Suppose 20 percent of all incoming email is spam, so the prior P(spam) is 0.20. The word free appears in 60 percent of spam emails, so the likelihood P(free given spam) is 0.60, and it appears in only 5 percent of legitimate emails, so P(free given not spam) is 0.05.

code.content:
p_spam = 0.20
p_not_spam = 1 - p_spam
p_free_given_spam = 0.60
p_free_given_not_spam = 0.05

p_free = p_free_given_spam * p_spam + p_free_given_not_spam * p_not_spam
p_spam_given_free = (p_free_given_spam * p_spam) / p_free
print(round(p_spam_given_free, 3))   # about 0.75

blocks.text: An email containing the word free jumps from a 20 percent prior chance of being spam to about 75 percent posterior chance once that single word is observed, a large but not overwhelming update, exactly the kind of number a real spam filter combines with many other words before making a final decision.

Real spam filters extend this same idea to dozens or hundreds of words at once, each word contributing its own likelihood ratio, and the naive Bayes assumption from the conditional probability lesson is precisely what allows all of those per word contributions to be multiplied together into one combined posterior instead of requiring an impossibly large table of every word combination.
11. Bayes Theorem and Naive Bayes Classifiers

The naive Bayes classifier introduced in the conditional probability lesson is named after exactly this formula. It computes P(class given features) using Bayes theorem, treating the prior as how common each class is overall, and the likelihood as how probable the observed features are given each class, then picking whichever class gives the highest posterior.

This is also why naive Bayes remains popular for text classification despite newer and more complex models existing, it is fast, requires very little training data to get reasonable estimates of each likelihood, and its predictions can be explained directly in terms of prior and likelihood values that are easy for a person to inspect.
11.1 Why the Evidence Term Can Be Skipped for Classification

For classification, only the relative order of the posteriors across classes matters, not their exact values, and since P(B), the evidence, is the same fixed number regardless of which class is being scored, naive Bayes implementations typically skip dividing by it entirely and simply compare P(B given A) times P(A) across classes, picking the largest.

code.content:
def naive_bayes_score(p_features_given_class, p_class):
    return p_features_given_class * p_class   # evidence term dropped, only used for ranking classes

spam_score = naive_bayes_score(0.60, 0.20)
not_spam_score = naive_bayes_score(0.05, 0.80)
print("spam" if spam_score > not_spam_score else "not spam")

blocks.text: 12. Prior Sensitivity: How the Prior Shapes the Posterior

Swapping in a different prior while keeping the likelihood fixed can shift the posterior dramatically, which is exactly why the rare disease example in section 7 works out so differently from what intuition expects. Because the prior does so much of the work, choosing a bad or outdated prior is one of the fastest ways to get a misleading posterior even with perfectly correct likelihoods.

Running the same likelihood and false positive rate across several different priors shows the posterior climbing steadily as the prior grows, from barely above zero when the condition is extremely rare to well above 90 percent once the condition is already fairly common, the exact opposite of a fixed universal posterior.

items: A prior estimated from a small or biased sample can distort every downstream posterior even when the likelihood is measured perfectly.
Priors that go stale, such as a disease prevalence measured years before a new outbreak, silently corrupt new predictions until they are refreshed.
When almost nothing is known in advance, a deliberately uninformative or flat prior is often used so the likelihood is left to do most of the work.

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example

A factory has two machines, Machine A produces 60 percent of parts with a 2 percent defect rate, and Machine B produces the remaining 40 percent of parts with a 5 percent defect rate, the same setup left unfinished at the end of the conditional probability lesson. A part is picked at random and found defective. What is the probability it came from Machine A.

code.content:
p_a = 0.60
p_b_machine = 0.40
p_defect_given_a = 0.02
p_defect_given_b = 0.05

p_defect = p_defect_given_a * p_a + p_defect_given_b * p_b_machine
p_a_given_defect = (p_defect_given_a * p_a) / p_defect
print(round(p_a_given_defect, 3))   # about 0.353

blocks.text: Even though Machine A makes the majority of parts, a defective part is only about 35.3 percent likely to have come from it, because Machine B, despite producing fewer parts overall, has a much higher defect rate, pulling more than its raw share of the blame once a defect is actually observed.

This result is worth comparing directly against the raw 60 percent versus 40 percent production split, the posterior of about 35.3 percent for Machine A sits noticeably below its 60 percent production share, exactly because Machine A defects are rarer per part than Machine B defects.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing the likelihood P(B given A) with the posterior P(A given B), exactly the reversal Bayes theorem exists to correct, and reporting the likelihood as if it already answered the real question.
Ignoring the prior entirely and reasoning only from the likelihood, which is precisely what makes the rare disease result in section 7 feel so surprising to first time readers.

Forgetting to compute the evidence term P(B) using the law of total probability, and instead dividing by only one branch of it, such as just P(B given A) times P(A) without adding the P(B given not A) term.
Applying a stale or poorly estimated prior long after the underlying population has shifted, silently making every downstream posterior wrong even though the formula itself is applied correctly.
Treating Bayes theorem as something exotic rather than recognizing it as a direct rearrangement of the general multiplication rule already covered in the conditional probability lesson.

blocks.text: A sixth closely related mistake worth naming separately is rounding intermediate probabilities too aggressively before the final division, since Bayes theorem often multiplies and divides several small numbers together, and early rounding can shift the final posterior by a surprisingly large amount.
15. Practice: Apply Bayes Theorem

A security system detects intrusions 95 percent of the time when an intrusion is actually happening, so the likelihood P(alarm given intrusion) is 0.95. It also false alarms 10 percent of the time when there is no intrusion, so P(alarm given no intrusion) is 0.10. Intrusions are rare, occurring only 2 percent of the time, so the prior P(intrusion) is 0.02. Compute P(intrusion given alarm).

code.content:
p_intrusion = 0.02
p_no_intrusion = 1 - p_intrusion
p_alarm_given_intrusion = 0.95
p_alarm_given_no_intrusion = 0.10

p_alarm = p_alarm_given_intrusion * p_intrusion + p_alarm_given_no_intrusion * p_no_intrusion
p_intrusion_given_alarm = (p_alarm_given_intrusion * p_intrusion) / p_alarm
print(round(p_intrusion_given_alarm, 4))

blocks.text: Compare the resulting posterior against the 95 percent likelihood used as an input, and notice how far below that number the true posterior lands, a pattern that should feel familiar after the medical test and spam filtering examples worked through earlier in this lesson.

As an extension, try recomputing the posterior after a second alarm assumed independent of the first, reusing the first posterior as the new prior exactly as demonstrated in the Bayesian updating section above, and compare how much faster the belief converges toward certainty than it did with the disease test example.
Key Takeaway

Bayes theorem, P(A given B) equals P(B given A) times P(A) divided by P(B), is nothing more than the general multiplication rule from the conditional probability lesson rearranged to solve for the reverse conditional probability, but that rearrangement is exactly what makes it so powerful, turning an easy to estimate likelihood into a hard to estimate posterior.

The prior, likelihood, evidence, and posterior terminology introduced here shows up throughout statistics and machine learning, from naive Bayes classifiers to Bayesian updating of beliefs as new data streams in, and the rare disease and spam filtering examples worked through in this lesson are the two patterns worth internalizing before moving on to the independence lesson, which asks the related question of when conditioning on one event leaves another event completely unchanged.
